title: This Year, Get Your Students Writing Provisionally
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart urges teachers to make daily "provisional writing" — low-stakes writing that exists only to make learning happen in the moment — the entry point for increasing student writing across the year, pointing to a priority pyramid from his book These 6 Things. He describes where provisional writing fits best (opening warm-ups, closing exit writes, mid-lesson transitions) and how flexible its purpose can be, from reviewing prior learning to reflecting on progress to making personal connections. He argues the practice pays off for teachers by normalizing writing and freeing up a few minutes to circulate and observe, and for students by building writing stamina and clarity about what they do and don't know. Crucially, he insists provisional writing should not be graded, since grading it would misrepresent the writing as being done for the teacher rather than for the writer's own growth, clarity, and power.
points: Provisional writing is defined narrowly and usefully: writing "that exists for today, for the purpose of making learning happen," not a graded product.

Stuart's placement guidance (start-of-class warm-up, end-of-class closer, or mid-lesson transition) gives teachers a concrete way to slot the practice into existing lesson structure without redesigning units.
He argues normalizing daily writing reduces student complaining over time because it becomes routine ("just what we do in here") rather than a special, resistible demand.
His core logistical rule — keep it simple (a spiral notebook, no grading) — removes the two most common reasons teachers cite for not doing this consistently.
quotes: This year, get your students writing more. It'll make your job easier, and it'll make their minds and hearts stronger.
This is called provisional writing — writing that exists for today, for the purpose of making learning happen.
As the act of writing becomes normalized in your classroom, student complaining diminishes. It becomes just "what we do" in here, not some anomaly to be protested.

As students are writing, you have a quiet moment to do a quick administrative task (e.g., quickly take attendance) and then (much more importantly) take a walk around the classroom to see how students are doing.

They become much clearer themselves on what they do and don't know. They overcome internal blocks to writing (e.g., "I can't write") because you've given them the opportunity and expectation and guidance and encouragement to write every single day.
Because it's provisional, there's no need to grade this. Grading it sends the wrong message, that this writing is something they are doing for you.
But what you want to communicate in word and deed is that writing is always first for the writer. The writer who gains power, clarity, wisdom, insight, and strength.
